pages.text:
*Garden Log, Day 220: Growing: everything. Someone came.*

The rain tapped against the glass of the Winter Room, a steady, rhythmic sound that usually helped me think. I was watering the ferns, counting the drops as they fell, when the heavy door creaked open. I dropped the can. Water splashed onto my boots, cold and sudden.

Mr. Osei stood in the doorway. He was wearing his blue overalls, and his cap was in his hands, held loosely at his sides. His shoulders were hunched, and he looked as if he had been standing there for a very long time, waiting for the rain to stop. It was not stopping.

He blinked, looking at the ferns, then at me, then at the wet floor. He shook his head, a small, slow movement, like a dog drying off, but slower.

"I heard the bench," he said.

His voice was rough, unused, like a lock that had not been turned in months. He did not step inside. He just stood in the doorway, letting the rain drip from his hair onto the concrete threshold. The garden hummed, a low, warm vibration that I could feel in my teeth. He looked at the ferns again. One of them, the tallest, was shaking its leaves, dropping water into the air.
pages.image: Mr. Osei, a tall man in blue overalls, stands in a wet doorway holding a cap, looking down at a shaking fern; rain drips from his hair, and a thin girl in a denim jacket watches from the garden path.

pages.text:
He stepped inside. Rain dripped from his boots, then stopped at the threshold. He moved slowly, hands hanging by his sides. He touched everything he passed. Fingers brushed the rough bark of the pear tree. A hand trailed along the ivy climbing the wall. He did not speak. He did not look at me. He was looking at the things, really looking, checking if they were still there.

In the Spring Room, he stopped.

There was a stone there, simple and grey, set into the earth. I had never seen him look at it before. He stood before it for a long time. The wind picked up outside, rattling the glass.

Then, the roses bloomed.

It was mid-January. Snow fell outside, soft and white against the dark. But inside, under the glass, every single rose on every bush opened at once. It was a sudden burst of red and pink, petals unfurling in a wave that moved from the far wall to the near one. The smell hit me first, thick and sweet, like the sugar in Baba’s bread mixed with rain. Mr. Osei stood very still, his hand flat on the stone.
pages.image: Mr. Osei stands still before a grey stone in a glass-walled garden, surrounded by a sudden burst of blooming red roses; snow falls outside the glass, contrasting with the vibrant flowers inside.

pages.text:
"They are late," he said, his voice barely louder than the water dripping from the ceiling. "They are always late."

I didn't answer. I remembered Mrs. Ilves on her sofa, her knitting needles clicking like a fast metronome. She had told me that some people build walls instead of doors because they think keeping things safe will stop them from breaking, but things break anyway, just quieter. Mr. Osei looked at his hands, rough and stained with old soil and oil.

"I couldn't come," he said. "Every time I looked at it, I saw what was missing."

He pressed his palm flat against the stone, his fingers spreading into the cold granite. "I built it so somebody would use it. I closed it so nobody could hurt it. I got it backwards."

The roses rustled, making a dry, papery sound. I wanted to tell him it was okay, but my mouth felt full of dirt. I just nodded, and he nodded back, slowly turning away from the stone.
pages.image: Mr. Osei presses his hand against a grey stone in a garden, his face profiled in soft light; red roses bloom in the background, and a girl in a denim jacket watches him with a thoughtful expression.

pages.text:
Gherkin was on the path. He had likely been there the entire time, though I had not seen him. He sat there as a small, mossy lump, his head raised and his eyes half-closed, watching Mr. Osei with a kind of bored patience.

"Mm," Gherkin said.

Mr. Osei stopped. He turned slowly, his boots scraping against the gravel, and looked down at the tortoise.

"I have been waiting for you," Gherkin said. "For thirty years."

Mr. Osei stared. His mouth opened, then closed again, leaving a small, silent gap.

"You are late," Gherkin continued. His voice carried a tone of mild annoyance, like a teacher checking a watch during a lesson, but not anger. "It is good to see you."

It was the longest sentence I had ever heard him say. It took him six minutes to finish. I counted the seconds, just to be sure.

Mr. Osei laughed. It was a short, sharp sound, like a crack in the glass. Then he cried. He laughed and cried at the same time, his shoulders shaking and his face crumpling in a way I had never seen before. It was messy and loud and completely real. He wiped his eyes with his sleeve, which was already covered in mud.

"I am sorry," he said to the tortoise. "I am sorry, Gherkin."

Gherkin blinked. "Mm. Not yet," he said, as if this were the only logical response.
pages.image: Gherkin, the hat-sized mossy tortoise, looks up at Mr. Osei, the very tall older man with a grey moustache in blue overalls, who wipes his eyes with a muddy sleeve, laughing and crying, while Sana in her denim jacket watches with a smile

pages.text:
Mr. Osei sat on the bench, which hummed under him with a low, warm note that seemed to steady his breathing. He stayed there for a long time, just listening to the rain fill the silence.

Finally, he looked at me.

"What do you want me to do?" he asked.

I took a breath, feeling my heart beat like a drum in my chest. I thought about the Council meeting, the notice on the door, and the fact that I was eleven and did not know how to save a garden.

"The Council is meeting in two weeks," I said. "They need to hear it. They need someone who built it. Someone who was here. Someone who knows what it is worth."

I looked down at my hands, which were dirty.

"I can't do it," I said. "I tried. I froze."

Mr. Osei looked at me. "My English," he said. "It is not good enough for meetings. I speak slowly. I make mistakes."

He paused, looking at the roses, then at the stone, then at me.

"I will try," he said.

It was the first true thing he had said to me, and the bench hummed louder for just a second before going quiet.
pages.image: Mr. Osei sits on a wooden bench in a glass garden, looking at a girl in a denim jacket; the background shows a rainy window and blooming roses, capturing a moment of quiet determination.
